topics.title: Chapter 1: Real Numbers
topics.description: Euclid's Division Lemma, HCF, Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, Decimals, and Irrational Numbers.

cards.heading: Euclid's Division Lemma
cards.conceptText: For any two positive integers 'a' and 'b', there exist unique integers 'q' and 'r' satisfying a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b. Here a = Dividend, b = Divisor, q = Quotient, and r = Remainder.

workedExample.problem: Express 17 divided by 5 in Euclid's form.

cards.keyTakeaway: The remainder (r) must always be strictly less than the divisor (b) and greater than or equal to zero (0 ≤ r < b).

cards.heading: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
cards.conceptText: Every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime powers, apart from the order of factors. For example, 72 = 2³ x 3².
cards.keyTakeaway: HCF = Product of smallest power of each common prime factor. LCM = Product of greatest power of each prime factor.

cards.heading: Terminating and Non-Terminating Repeating Decimals
cards.conceptText: A rational number p/q in simplest form has a terminating decimal expansion if and only if the denominator q has prime factorisation of the form 2ⁿ · 5ᵐ (where n, m are non-negative integers).

workedExample.problem: Does 13/25 have a terminating decimal representation?
steps: Denominator is of the form 2ⁿ · 5ᵐ (n=0, m=2)
workedExample.finalAnswer: It has a terminating decimal representation.

cards.keyTakeaway: The denominator must only contain prime factors of 2 and/or 5. If any other prime factor (such as 3, 7, 11) is present, it is non-terminating repeating.

topics.title: Chapter 2: Sets & Polynomials
topics.description: Set representations, Union, Intersection, Difference of Sets, Venn Diagrams, and Zeroes of Polynomials.

cards.heading: Union of Sets (A ∪ B)
cards.conceptText: The union of sets A and B contains all elements that belong to A, B, or both. A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}. Repetitions are counted only once.

workedExample.problem: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}, find A ∪ B.

cards.keyTakeaway: Union brings everything together: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B).

cards.heading: Intersection of Sets (A ∩ B)
cards.conceptText: The intersection of sets A and B contains only elements that belong to both A and B. If A ∩ B = ∅, they are disjoint sets.

steps: Compare elements of A and B
Common elements present in both sets are 4 and 8

cards.keyTakeaway: Intersection takes only what is strictly common to both sets.

cards.heading: Difference of Sets (A - B)
cards.conceptText: The set difference A - B is the set of elements that belong to A but not to B. A - B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
cards.keyTakeaway: A - B is not equal to B - A. Select only elements belonging strictly to the first set.

questions.text: In Euclid's Division Lemma a = bq + r, what condition must the remainder 'r' satisfy?
hintLadder: The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor 'b', and it can also be zero.
Zero or greater (0 ≤ r), and strictly less than divisor (< b).
The exact mathematical condition is 0 ≤ r < b. Hence Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: According to Euclid's Division Lemma, the remainder r always satisfies 0 ≤ r < b.

questions.text: When 37 is divided by 7, what are the quotient q and remainder r in the form a = bq + r?
hintLadder: Recall multiplication table of 7: 7 x 5 = 35. Subtract 35 from 37.
37 = (7 x 5) + 2. Here 2 is less than 7 (0 ≤ 2 < 7).
Therefore, quotient q = 5 and remainder r = 2. Option B is correct.

questions.text: When any positive integer 'a' is divided by 4, what are the possible values for the remainder r?
hintLadder: The condition is 0 ≤ r < 4.
r can take values starting from 0 up to 3.
Since r < 4, r cannot be 4. The possible values are 0, 1, 2, 3. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: Since divisor b = 4, 0 ≤ r < 4 gives r ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}.

questions.text: What is the HCF of 12 and 18 using Euclid's division algorithm?
hintLadder: Now divide 12 by the remainder 6: 12 = 6(2) + 0.
The remainder is 0. The divisor at this stage is 6. Option B is correct.

questions.text: What is the HCF of 45 and 105 using Euclid's method?
hintLadder: Step 2: Divide 45 by 15: 45 = 15(3) + 0.
The remainder reached 0. The divisor is 15. Hence HCF is 15. Option B is correct.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct prime factorisation of 36?
hintLadder: Divide 36 by primes: 36 = 2 x 18 = 2 x 2 x 9.
Factor 9: 9 = 3 x 3.
Therefore, 36 = 2² x 3². Note that 4 and 6 are composite numbers, not primes. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: Prime factorisation requires prime bases only: 36 = 2² x 3².

questions.text: If HCF(a, b) = 6 and LCM(a, b) = 36, and a = 12, what is the value of b?
hintLadder: Use the fundamental relation: a x b = HCF x LCM.
Substitute values: 12 x b = 6 x 36 = 216.
b = 216 ÷ 12 = 18. Option A is correct.
questions.explanation: a x b = HCF x LCM => 12 x b = 6 x 36 => b = 18.

questions.text: Which of the following fractions has a terminating decimal representation?
hintLadder: Inspect the prime factors of the denominators.
15 = 3 x 5 (contains 3), 3 = 3, 14 = 2 x 7 (contains 7).
Denominator of 3/8 is 8 = 2³. Since it has only 2s in its factorisation, 3/8 is terminating (0.375). Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: Denominator 8 = 2³ contains only prime factor 2. Thus 3/8 is terminating.

questions.text: After how many decimal places will the decimal representation of 17 / (2² x 5³) terminate?
hintLadder: Observe the powers of 2 and 5 in the denominator: 2² and 5³.
The number of decimal places is determined by the maximum power: max(2, 3).
Here max(2, 3) = 3. Therefore it terminates after 3 decimal places. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: Max power of 2 and 5 in denominator is 3. Hence it terminates after 3 places.

questions.text: Which of the following numbers is an irrational number?
hintLadder: Calculate square roots: √4 = 2, √9 = 3, √16 = 4 (all integers / rational).
5 is not a perfect square, so √5 cannot be written as p/q.
Therefore √5 is an irrational number. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: √5 is non-terminating and non-recurring; it is irrational.

questions.text: If A = {x : x is a prime number less than 10}, what is the roster form of set A?
hintLadder: Remember: 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Primes less than 10 are: 2, 3, 5, 7 (9 is composite because 3 x 3 = 9).
Therefore A = {2, 3, 5, 7}. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: The prime numbers under 10 are strictly 2, 3, 5, and 7.

questions.text: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}, what is A ∪ B?
hintLadder: Union brings together all elements from both sets.
Common elements like 3 are written only once.
Combining without repetition gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with no duplicate entries.

questions.text: If A = {a, b, c, d} and B = {c, d, e, f}, what is A ∩ B?
hintLadder: Intersection takes elements that appear in both sets.
Elements in both A and B are c and d.
Therefore A ∩ B = {c, d}. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: Only 'c' and 'd' belong to both sets A and B.

hintLadder: A - B means elements belonging to A but not to B.
Start with A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Remove 3 and 4 because they are in B.
Remaining elements: {1, 2}. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: A - B contains elements exclusive to A: {1, 2}.

questions.text: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5, 6} (disjoint sets), what is A - B?
hintLadder: Notice that A and B have no common elements at all (A ∩ B = ∅).
Since none of A's elements are in B, nothing is removed from A.
Therefore A - B = A. Option B is correct.
questions.explanation: When A and B are disjoint, no elements are removed from A, so A - B = A.

mistakeRemedies.forgot_remainder: Remember that the remainder must always be strictly less than the divisor (0 ≤ r < b). Never omit the remainder.
mistakeRemedies.remainder_greater_than_divisor: The remainder cannot be greater than the divisor! If dividing by 7, remainder must be between 0 and 6.
mistakeRemedies.wrong_multiplication: Check your multiplication table. The quotient multiplied by divisor must be as close to the dividend as possible without exceeding it.
mistakeRemedies.remainder_equals_divisor: The remainder can never equal the divisor. If it does, the quotient should increase by 1.
mistakeRemedies.included_equal_to_b: The remainder 'r' cannot equal 'b', it must be strictly less than b (< b).
mistakeRemedies.forgot_zero_remainder: The remainder can be 0 when the division is exact (r = 0).
mistakeRemedies.included_divisor_itself: The divisor itself is never a valid remainder. Dividing by 4 gives remainders 0, 1, 2, 3.
mistakeRemedies.missed_zero: Zero is a valid remainder: 0 ≤ r < b.
mistakeRemedies.not_highest_common_factor: The factor you found is common, but it is not the highest common factor (HCF).
mistakeRemedies.incomplete_factor: A larger common factor exists. Continue Euclid's division until remainder is 0.
mistakeRemedies.chose_smaller_number: The smaller number is not automatically the HCF. Complete the division algorithm.
mistakeRemedies.partial_factor: This is only a partial factor. Take the final non-zero divisor.
mistakeRemedies.chose_first_remainder: The first remainder is not the HCF. The divisor at the step where remainder becomes 0 is the HCF.
mistakeRemedies.missed_power_of_two: Check how many times 2 divides the number. Don't forget the power exponent.
mistakeRemedies.squared_wrong_factor: Make sure to attach the power to the exact prime factor being multiplied.
mistakeRemedies.used_composite_numbers: Prime factorisation must use prime numbers only (2, 3, 5, 7...). Do not leave 4, 6, 9 as bases.
mistakeRemedies.divided_by_hcf_twice: Use formula: a x b = HCF x LCM. Therefore b = (HCF x LCM) ÷ a.
mistakeRemedies.assumed_ends_with_zero: To end with the digit 0, the prime factorisation must contain both 2 and 5.
mistakeRemedies.contains_factor_3: Because 3 is in the denominator, this is non-terminating repeating. Terminating decimals require only 2 or 5 in the denominator.
mistakeRemedies.contains_factor_7: A factor of 7 in the denominator makes it non-terminating repeating.
mistakeRemedies.contains_factor_11: A factor of 11 in denominator means it cannot terminate.
mistakeRemedies.chose_difference: The number of places is not the difference between powers, but the maximum power: max(n, m).
mistakeRemedies.chose_smaller_power: Take the maximum power of 2 and 5, not the smaller power.
mistakeRemedies.added_the_powers: Do not add the powers. Take max(n, m).
mistakeRemedies.perfect_square_4: 4 is a perfect square (2² = 4), so √4 = 2 is a rational number.
mistakeRemedies.perfect_square_9: 9 is a perfect square (3² = 9), so √9 = 3 is rational.
mistakeRemedies.perfect_square_16: 16 is a perfect square (4² = 16), so √16 = 4 is rational.
mistakeRemedies.assumed_rational_dominates: Adding or subtracting a rational and an irrational number always yields an irrational number.
mistakeRemedies.counted_duplicates: Elements in a set are listed without repetition.
mistakeRemedies.chose_element_count: Number of subsets is given by 2ⁿ, not n.
mistakeRemedies.missed_empty_set: The empty set (∅) is always a subset of every set.
mistakeRemedies.calculated_A_minus_B_instead: Notice the question asked for B - A, not A - B.
mistakeRemedies.chose_common_elements: That is the intersection A ∩ B, not the difference.
mistakeRemedies.difference_swap: A - B is different from B - A. Always take elements belonging only to the first set.
mistakeRemedies.assumed_nothing_left: There are elements remaining in the first set.
mistakeRemedies.swapped_with_B: Make sure you keep the elements of the first set.
mistakeRemedies.confused_with_union: Do not combine the sets; this is a set difference.

commonDoubts.q: How to quickly check if a fraction has a terminating decimal?
commonDoubts.a: Reduce the fraction to lowest terms. Then factorise the denominator. If the denominator has ONLY prime factors 2 and/or 5 (form 2ⁿ · 5ᵐ), it terminates. If it contains 3, 7, 11 etc., it is non-terminating repeating.

commonDoubts.q: What is Euclid's Division Lemma used for?
commonDoubts.a: Euclid's Division Lemma states that for any two positive integers a and b, a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b. It is primarily used to systematically compute the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two large numbers.

commonDoubts.q: Why is the square root of 2 or 3 irrational?
commonDoubts.a: Because they cannot be written in the form p/q where p and q are co-prime integers. When assumed rational, proof by contradiction reveals that both p and q would share a common factor, violating the definition.

commonDoubts.q: What is the difference between A - B and B - A?
commonDoubts.a: A - B contains elements that belong to A but NOT to B. B - A contains elements that belong to B but NOT to A. They are not equal unless A and B are identical sets.
Two sets A and B are disjoint if they share no elements in common. Mathematically, their intersection is the empty set: A ∩ B = ∅.
